story-anscombe.script: Here's a story from 1973 that I absolutely love. A statistician named Francis Anscombe built four little datasets that were statistical twins — identical mean, identical variance, identical correlation, even the same best-fit line. On paper, you couldn't tell them apart. But then he plotted them, and one was a clean line, one a curve, one had a wild outlier, one nearly vertical. The numbers hid everything, and in Lab 2 you'll prove this yourself instead of just taking my word for it.

concept-charts-argue.script: Here's a way to think about charts that will save you a lot of wasted effort: every chart is really an argument, an answer to a question you can say in one sentence. A histogram answers "how is one variable spread out?" — where do my detection distances pile up? A scatter asks "how do two things relate?" — does confidence drop as objects shrink? And correlation squeezes that relationship into a single number. If you can't state the sentence, you don't need the chart.

concept-chart-map.script: Here's a simple truth about charts: the question you're asking decides which one to use. Tracking something over time? That's a line chart. Comparing categories, like how many of each object you detected? Reach for a bar chart. Want to show a relationship between two things, like study hours and grades? A scatter plot. And be careful with pie charts—our eyes are terrible at judging angles, so bars almost always win. State your question first, and the chart picks itself.

quiz-chart-choice.script: Let's think about this carefully. Your claim connects two things — how big an object is, and how confident the detector feels about it. When you're arguing about a relationship between two variables, the scatter plot is your tool, because it shows every point and reveals the shape. Now watch out for that bar chart of averages — it feels tempting, but averaging first quietly erases the very pattern you're trying to prove. And time? That's not even part of your claim, so don't be fooled.

concept-anscombe-visual.script: Look closely at these four pictures, because something amazing is happening here. All four have the exact same average, the same correlation, and the same best-fit line — the numbers are identical. But the shapes could not be more different: one is a clean line, one is actually a smooth curve, one has a single rogue point bending everything, and in the last, one lonely point invents the whole correlation by itself. So please, always plot your data before you trust any statistic about it — describe() is where looking begins, never where it ends.

concept-correlation.script: Here's a neat idea: we can capture an entire relationship in a single number called r. When r is near positive one, two things rise together tightly, like study hours and grades; near negative one, one climbs as the other falls; and near zero, there's just no straight-line pattern at all. But watch out for two traps: first, correlation never proves causation — ice-cream sales and drownings rise together because summer drives both. Second, r only sees straight lines, so a perfect curve can fool it completely, which is why the fix is always the same: plot it.

quiz-correlation.script: Here's a classic trap for you. Cities with more firefighters really do have more fire damage — the correlation is strong and genuine. So should we fire the firefighters to stop the damage? Of course not! There's a lurking variable hiding here: bigger fires bring more firefighters and more damage at the same time. The number tells you things move together, but it never proves one causes the other — and to actually test a cause, we'll need experiments, which is exactly where we're headed in Class 14.

concept-honest-axes.script: Look closely at these two charts, because they show the exact same numbers — 88, 90, and 92 percent. On the left, where the axis starts at zero, the three detectors look nearly tied, which is the truth. But on the right, where the axis starts at 87, detector C suddenly looks three times better, even though nothing about the data changed. That's the oldest trick in the book, and you'll spot it everywhere once you know to check whether the axis starts at a sensible value, whether the units are labeled, and whether the caption speaks for itself.

reference-key-terms.script: Let me leave you with a handful of terms that will actually change how you see the world this week. A histogram shows the shape of one variable, while a scatter plot reveals the relationship between two. Correlation, that number between minus one and one, tells you how strong a straight-line link is — but it never tells you why. Watch closely for two things: a lurking variable, the hidden cause behind a surprising connection, and a truncated axis, where someone chops off zero to make tiny differences look huge. Those last two are the tricks you'll spot on the news and on your feed all the time.

backup-liars-gallery.script: Let me show you three tricks that turn honest data into lies. First, the truncated axis: start the y-axis at 87 instead of zero, and tiny differences suddenly look huge, so always read the axis numbers first. Second, the cherry-picked window, where "sales up 40 percent" just means they started counting right after a crash, so ask what the graph looks like if you extend it further back. Third, the double y-axis, where two unrelated scales get stacked until they seem to move together, so demand each story separately. And remember, a chart is a claim, so apply the same verification you'd give any text: who made this, what's the source, what would the honest version look like?
